section_title: Why are the kings gathered, and why does Jesus interrupt with a warning?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 12 And the sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East. 13 And I saw three unclean spirits that looked like frogs coming out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet. 14 These are demonic spirits that perform signs and go out to all the kings of the earth, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.

15 “Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who remains awake and clothed, so that he will not go naked and let his shame be exposed.” 16 And they assembled the kings in the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.

context_lines: The sixth bowl dries the Euphrates, preparing the way for the kings of the East. John then sees three unclean spirits like frogs coming from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet. He identifies them directly as demonic spirits that perform signs and draw the world’s kings toward battle.

Their gathering is for the great day of God Almighty. The powers are deceived into assembling, yet the day is still named for God. The vision does not suggest that their combined strength places the outcome beyond His authority.

In the middle of the scene, Jesus warns that He is coming like a thief and blesses the person who remains awake and clothed. The warning addresses readiness and faithfulness while the world is being drawn into deception. Attention shifts briefly from what the kings are doing to how His people should live.

The gathering place is called Armageddon. The name is commonly linked with Megiddo, although its exact derivation is debated; see [Thayer’s discussion](https://biblehub.com/greek/717.htm). The passage names the gathering but does not yet narrate the battle itself.
common_interpretation_lines: The kings from the East receive different identifications. The [USCCB notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/revelation/16) relate them to the Parthians in the setting of the Roman world. [Walvoord](https://swartzentrover.com/cotor/E-Books/holiness/Walvoord/Revelation/Rev_16.htm) expects future eastern rulers approaching the final conflict. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ/) also expects an eastern advance, while connecting it with his wider account of the powers opposed to God. The passage itself does not name a modern nation.

The unclean spirits need less reconstruction: John identifies them as demons and explains their deceptive signs and mission. The name Armageddon is variously understood as pointing to a future military gathering around Megiddo or as a picture of the final overthrow of hostile powers, drawing on the place’s biblical associations.

The warning about coming like a thief is understood as a call to watchfulness. It does not give a date for the gathering or invite readers to calculate one from a current event. Faithful readiness remains the stated blessing.
god_plan_lines: The drying of water recalls [Exodus 14:21–28](https://biblehub.com/bsb/exodus/14.htm), where a path opens through the sea but the pursuing army meets destruction. This is a scriptural parallel rather than an identical event: in Revelation, the opened way brings hostile rulers toward the day of God’s reckoning. Their movement does not amount to victory over Him.

The interruption also repeats the warning Jesus gave in [Matthew 24:42–44](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/24.htm), where the unexpected thief illustrates the need to be ready for the Son of Man. The same theme appears in [Revelation 3:3](https://biblehub.com/bsb/revelation/3.htm). Within the larger picture of judgment, His people are called to remain awake and faithful.
